name: Chottanikkara Bhagavathy Temple (Sri Rajarajeswari)
deity: The presiding goddess is Sri Bhagavathy, worshipped as Sri Rajarajeswari, a form of Adi Parashakti, the Mother Goddess. Devotees address her affectionately as Chottanikkara Amma.
summary: Chottanikkara Bhagavathy Temple, near Kochi, is one of Kerala's most revered shrines to the Mother Goddess. The Devi is honoured here as Sri Rajarajeswari, and the temple is known across the region as a place where the distressed come seeking solace.

sections.history: Chottanikkara has been a living centre of Devi worship for many centuries, and tradition holds the site to be far older than surviving records can confirm. Over generations it grew from a local shrine into one of Kerala's foremost goddess temples, sustained by the devotion of ordinary pilgrims and the patronage of regional rulers who endowed its rituals and upkeep. The temple's enduring fame rests less on royal monuments than on the continuity of daily worship and the accounts of devotees who found relief here. Its two shrines, the upper Melkavu and the lower Keezhkavu, together shaped a distinctive tradition of worship that has drawn seekers from far beyond the surrounding villages.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the characteristic idiom of Kerala sacred architecture, with a sanctum crowned by a sloping tiled roof designed for the heavy monsoon and finished in traditional woodwork. The complex centres on two shrines: the upper Melkavu, dedicated to Sri Rajarajeswari, and the lower Keezhkavu, associated with Bhadrakali, set a short distance apart. Timber columns, carved brackets and copper-clad roofing reflect the region's building conventions, while the surrounding walls and lamp-lined pathways frame the ritual space. The layout is unassuming rather than monumental, its atmosphere shaped by oil lamps, the murmur of chanting and the ordered rhythm of daily rites rather than by ornament alone.
sections.legends: Chottanikkara is celebrated in tradition as a refuge for those troubled in mind and spirit. A distinctive practice marks the Devi's presence through the day: she is revered in the morning as Saraswati, robed in white; at noon as Bhadrakali, or Lakshmi, in crimson; and in the evening as Durga, in blue. The lower Keezhkavu shrine is bound to accounts of devotees seeking release from affliction, and its evening Guruthi observance is closely linked to this belief. Many stories passed down among pilgrims tell of relief found after prayer here, and it is this reputation, more than any single episode, that has made the goddess of Chottanikkara so widely invoked.
sections.festivals: The foremost festival is Makam Thozhal, observed on the Makam star in the Malayalam month of Kumbham, when the Devi is believed to grant a specially auspicious darshan and vast crowds gather for the sight. The annual festival week is celebrated with processions, traditional music and ritual offerings, drawing devotees from across Kerala and beyond. Navaratri, sacred to the Mother Goddess, is another season of particular significance, marked by special worship over its nine nights. Throughout the year the daily rites, including the evening observances at the Keezhkavu, sustain the temple's rhythm between these larger occasions.
sections.experience: A visit to Chottanikkara is shaped by the quiet intensity of a working Devi temple rather than by spectacle. Pilgrims move between the upper and lower shrines, many arriving with private burdens they hope to set down before the goddess. Mornings carry the freshness of the first worship, while evenings, lit by rows of oil lamps and marked by the Keezhkavu observances, hold a gravity of their own. The changing adornment of the Devi through the day gives each visit a different mood. Amid the sound of bells and chanting, the experience is less about grandeur and more about the sense of nearness to a mother figure that draws people back.

visit.timings: The temple generally opens in the early morning and again in the evening, following Kerala temple custom, with a midday break. Exact hours and puja times vary by season and festival, so please verify locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Traditional, modest dress is expected. Men commonly wear a mundu and women a saree or comparable attire, in keeping with Kerala temple convention.
visit.photography: Photography is typically restricted inside the shrines and around the sanctum. Please follow posted notices and the instructions of temple staff.
visit.gettingThere: Chottanikkara lies near Kochi in Ernakulam district. The nearest major railhead is Ernakulam, and the nearest airport is Kochi (Nedumbassery); the temple is well connected by road.
